Create a family specification for graphs of families of hypotheses

Source: R/family_spec.R
family_spec.Rd

A family specification groups hypotheses into families. When it is passed to graph_optimise() or calc_power_pvals(), each node of the graph is a family rather than a single hypothesis, and the graph is tested with the procedure of Maurer and Bretz (2014):

Usage

family_spec(members, ..., test = "hommel")

Arguments

members

A list of integer vectors, one per family, giving the hypotheses (columns of the p-value matrix) in each family. Together they must contain each of 1, ..., m exactly once. If the list is named, the names are used as family names; otherwise families are named "F1", "F2", and so on.

...

These dots are for future extensions and must be empty.

test

The within-family test: "hommel" (default), "hochberg" or "holm". Either a single test used for every family, or one test per family.

Value

A multigrain_family_spec object containing:

  • members: a named list with the (sorted) hypotheses in each family.

  • test: a named character vector with the within-family test of each family.

Details

  • within a family, the hypotheses are tested with test at the family's local significance level;

  • a family passes its weight on only when every hypothesis in it is rejected.

Families are combined with a weighted Bonferroni test, as the hypotheses of a standard graph are. Within each family, test is applied to that family's p-values alone:

  • "hommel": the Hommel (1988) procedure, i.e. the closed test with Simes intersection tests.

  • "hochberg": the Hochberg (1988) step-up procedure.

  • "holm": the Holm (1979) step-down procedure.

Hommel and Hochberg control the family-wise error rate when the test statistics within a family are positively dependent, for example one-sided tests based on multivariate normal statistics with non-negative correlations. This cannot be checked from the p-values; use "holm" for a family where negative dependence is possible. For a family with a single hypothesis every test gives the same result.

The hypotheses are the columns of the p-value matrix. In trial_success(), r1, r2, ... still refer to these individual hypotheses; the success of a whole family is written as a conjunction, for example r2 && r3.

References

Maurer, W. and Bretz, F. (2014). A note on testing families of hypotheses using graphical procedures. Statistics in Medicine, 33(30), 5340–5346. doi:10.1002/sim.6307

Hommel, G. (1988). A stagewise rejective multiple test procedure based on a modified Bonferroni test. Biometrika, 75(2), 383–386. doi:10.1093/biomet/75.2.383

Hochberg, Y. (1988). A sharper Bonferroni procedure for multiple tests of significance. Biometrika, 75(4), 800–802. doi:10.1093/biomet/75.4.800

Holm, S. (1979). A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics, 6(2), 65–70.

See also

graph_optimise() and calc_power_pvals(), which take the family specification through their families argument.

Examples

# Five hypotheses in three families: H1 alone, H2 to H4 together and H5
# alone. Hommel is used within every family.
family_spec(list(primary = 1, secondary = 2:4, other = 5))
#> <multigrain_family_spec>
#> Hypotheses (columns of the p-value matrix) in each family:
#> primary   (hommel): 1
#> secondary (hommel): 2 3 4
#> other     (hommel): 5

# One test per family
family_spec(
  list(primary = 1, secondary = 2:4, other = 5),
  test = c("hommel", "hochberg", "holm")
)
#> <multigrain_family_spec>
#> Hypotheses (columns of the p-value matrix) in each family:
#> primary   (hommel): 1
#> secondary (hochberg): 2 3 4
#> other     (holm): 5
